children: The airline sector was impacted immeasurably by September 11, 2011. The attacks began with the hijacking of American Airlines Flight 11, American Airlines Flight 77, United Airlines Flight 93, and United Airlines Flight 175. The FAA began progressively restricting U.S. flying after the attacks began, then issued the decisive nationwide ground stop order at 9:42 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time, less than one hour after American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center. It was two days later that U.S. national airspace began to reopen.

Following a four-day closure, U.S. markets reopened on Monday, September 17, and airline stocks were among the hardest hit, including a 30% decline for American Airlines and a 42% slide for United Airlines as investors priced in an abrupt collapse in air travel, high fixed costs, operational disruption, and a heightened risk that financially weak carriers would fail.

Two major U.S. carriers went bankrupt as a direct result of 9/11. US Airways filed first, in August 2002, after the attacks forced an extended closure of its Reagan National hub on top of a merger with United Airlines that had already fallen apart. United followed in December 2002 in one of the largest bankruptcies in U.S. history, having lost two of the four hijacked planes and seeing demand collapse afterward. United did not emerge from bankruptcy until 2006, after cutting 30% of its jobs and terminating its pension plan.

Delta and Northwest both filed three years later, on the same day in September 2005, after a jet-fuel price spike linked to Hurricane Katrina pushed them to the brink. America West came close to the same bankruptcy fate but was kept alive by a federal loan guarantee, later merging into a bankrupt US Airways anyway. American Airlines was the outlier, avoiding bankruptcy entirely in that era by negotiating deep union concessions in 2003 and not filing until 2011 for unrelated reasons.
Major consolidation followed the bankruptcy wave, including pairings of America West-US Airways, Delta-Northwest, United-Continental, and American-US Airways.
each operated through the post-9/11 period without filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

After 9/11, airport security became federally managed through the TSA, with stricter passenger and baggage screening, ID checks, prohibited-item rules, and much less access to airport gates for nontravelers. Aircraft also received reinforced, locked cockpit doors and more air marshals. Watchlist checks also became more prominent. Since 9/11, flying has permanently become a more security-focused, time-consuming process for passengers and a more tightly regulated business for airlines.
